title: The Bronze Altar, the Courtyard, and Oil for the Lamps
summary: God gives the design for the altar of burnt offering: a hollow square box of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, with a horn on each corner, a bronze grate, and poles for carrying. He then describes the courtyard around the tabernacle, a hundred cubits by fifty, enclosed by linen curtains hung on posts in bronze bases, with an embroidered gate on the east. Finally he commands pure olive oil so that Aaron and his sons can keep the lamps burning before the LORD from evening until morning.
story: Chapters 25-26 moved from the ark outward to the tent; chapter 27 steps outside the tent into the courtyard, the space ordinary Israelites could enter. The bronze altar stood between the gate and the tent, so no one could approach the dwelling of God without passing the place of sacrifice. This altar will be the center of the offerings laid out in Leviticus 1-7. The chapter's last two verses turn back inside to the lamps and name, for the first time in this section, the ones who tend them, Aaron and his sons. That leads straight into chapter 28 on the priests' clothing and chapter 29 on their ordination.
historical:
Horned altars are well attested in ancient Israel and among its neighbors. Excavations at Megiddo uncovered limestone altars with horns at their corners, and at Tel Beersheba archaeologists found the dressed stones of a large four-horned altar reused in the wall of a storehouse. Many connect its dismantling with the reforms of Hezekiah in the late eighth century BC, who removed outlying altars and told Judah to worship “before this altar in Jerusalem” (2 Kings 18:22). The horns carried real weight. A man fleeing for his life could take hold of them to claim sanctuary, as Adonijah and later Joab did at the start of Solomon's reign (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28), and the priest put blood from the sin offering on them (Leviticus 4:25).

The measurements give a sense of scale. With a cubit of about 18 inches (45 centimeters), the altar was about 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) square and 4.5 feet (1.4 meters) high. The courtyard measured about 150 by 75 feet (46 by 23 meters), enclosed by curtains about 7.5 feet high, too tall to see over, so the sanctuary was hidden from the camp until one came through the gate.
cultural:
Every tool in this chapter serves the work of sacrifice: pots for ashes, shovels, sprinkling bowls for the blood, meat forks, and firepans. The altar was a place of fire, blood, smoke, and butchery, a working hearth of worship rather than a quiet shrine. The bronze grate halfway up probably held the fire and let air reach it, and the ledge may have given the priests a place to stand. The posts of the courtyard had bronze bases and silver hooks and bands, and the tent pegs of verse 19 remind the reader that this was a camp, struck and pitched again each time Israel moved.

The lamp oil was to be “pure oil of pressed olives” (verse 20), literally beaten oil: olives crushed lightly in a mortar rather than pressed hard, yielding the first and clearest oil, which burned brightly with little smoke. It was costly, and the command says it is to come from the Israelites as a whole, so every household had a share in the light that burned before the LORD through the night.
literary: The chapter has three parts: the altar (verses 1-8), the courtyard (verses 9-19), and the lamp oil (verses 20-21). The altar section ends, like the ark and the tent before it, with the reminder that it must be made as Moses was shown on the mountain (verse 8). The courtyard section reads like a surveyor's plan, walking the perimeter south, north, west, and east before giving the totals (verse 18). The last two verses break the pattern of construction. They introduce the first permanent statute of the tabernacle's worship, the word tamid (continually), the priests Aaron and his sons, and the name Tent of Meeting, which appears here for the first time in the Bible and will become the tabernacle's most common name.

outline.t: The bronze altar of burnt offering
The courtyard's south, north, west, and east sides
The gate and the full measure of the court
Oil for the lamps that burn continually

doctrines.note: The altar stood between the gate and the tent, so every approach to God passed the place of sacrifice, and its horns received the blood of sin offerings. The layout itself teaches that sinners come near to a holy God only by way of a life given.

The courtyard curtains mark off holy ground within the camp and hide the sanctuary from casual view. The graded spaces, from camp to court to tent to inner room, teach that God's presence is near but never common.

The oil came from all the Israelites, and the priests tended the lamps on behalf of the whole people. Worship at the sanctuary belonged to the whole community, not only to specialists, and the risen Christ later calls his churches lampstands (Revelation 1:20).

words.note: Mizbeach, altar, from zavach, to slaughter for sacrifice: literally a place of slaughter. The altar of burnt offering was the largest object in the sanctuary and the first a worshiper met inside the gate. Later texts call it the bronze altar, to distinguish it from the golden altar of incense inside the tent (30:1-10).

Qeren, horn. In the Old Testament a horn is an image of strength, and a raised horn means power and victory. The altar's four horns were its most holy points, receiving the blood of sin offerings and the grip of those seeking refuge. Zechariah praises God for raising up “a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David” (Luke 1:69).

Tamid, continually or regularly. The lamps are to burn tamid, and verse 21 defines it as from evening until morning, a regular, unbroken practice night after night rather than a flame that never went out. The same word describes the daily burnt offering (29:38-42) and the Bread of the Presence (25:30), and in later Judaism Tamid became the name of the twice-daily sacrifice.

christ: Hebrews claims this altar's meaning for Christ. “We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat” (Hebrews 13:10), it says, and it explains that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The bronze altar's sacrifices were offered day after day, and Hebrews contrasts them with Christ, who “offered for all time one sacrifice for sins” and then sat down (Hebrews 10:11-12). The link between the altar and the cross is not a code hidden in Exodus 27; it is the New Testament's claim that what the altar did provisionally, again and again, Christ did once. The lamps have their own echo. In Revelation the risen Christ walks among the lampstands that are his churches and warns that a church that will not repent may lose its lampstand (Revelation 2:5).

hard.q: How does a wooden altar covered in bronze fit the command in 20:24-25 for an altar of earth or uncut stone?
hard.a: Exodus 20:24-25 calls for an altar of earth, or of stones untouched by tools, while chapter 27 describes a finished box of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. Several explanations are offered. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, suggest that the hollow frame of verse 8 was filled with earth or rough stones wherever it was set up, so that the fire burned on earth and the bronze box served as a portable casing; on this reading the two laws describe one altar. Others take 20:24-25 as the rule for the simple altars built wherever God caused his name to be remembered, as when Joshua built on Mount Ebal “an altar of uncut stones on which no iron tool has been used” (Joshua 8:31), while chapter 27 governs the single altar of the central sanctuary. Critical scholars often assign the two laws to different sources and periods, one reflecting local altars and the other a priestly, centralized worship. Both texts share one concern: the altar is built on God's terms, not as a display of human craft or power.

questions: No one could reach the tent of God's presence without passing the altar of sacrifice. What does that arrangement say about how people come near to God?
The whole people brought the oil, and the priests kept the lamps burning through the night. What is your share in keeping a community's worship alive?
The courtyard was a working space of fire, blood, and ash. How does that challenge the idea that worship should always be tidy and comfortable?
